planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this alba blooms later in the season than most of its class.

directions: An Alba rose introduced in France in the 1870s, Pompon Blanc Parfait bears very double, blush-white pompon-form blooms held in dense, tidy clusters above soft grey-green alba foliage. Like other Albas it flowers once in early summer but is notably later and longer-blooming than most of its class, with a light, clean fragrance. It is exceptionally cold-hardy and disease-resistant, tolerating poor soil, partial shade, and neglect better than almost any other old rose. Prune only lightly after flowering to remove dead or crossing wood.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this striped Gallica stays compact and suckers less than many of its class.

directions: Raised in Belgium and introduced by Van Houtte in 1846, Tricolore de Flandre is a striped Gallica whose semi-double to double blooms are splashed with purple, lilac-pink, and white over a blush background, no two flowers quite alike. Gallicas are among the oldest garden roses in cultivation, prized for their compact, dense habit and strong old-rose fragrance. It flowers once, in a single heavy flush in early summer, and tolerates lean soil far better than modern repeat-blooming roses. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this small-flowered Gallica forms a dense, twiggy thicket.

directions: Raised by Vibert in France in 1845, Perle des Panachees is a petite-flowered striped Gallica, its small double blooms streaked irregularly in white, pink, and deep rose-red. Like other Gallicas it suckers to form a dense, twiggy thicket and flowers once in early summer with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. It is cold-hardy and tolerant of poor soil, needing only the removal of dead or crossing canes after its bloom flush. Its intricate, almost hand-painted petal markings make it a favorite among collectors of striped old roses.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this old rose is grown chiefly for its unusual color-changing blooms.

directions: The Bishop is an old European rose of uncertain origin, long grown as a Gallica, prized for semi-double rosette blooms that open rich magenta-crimson and age through violet to a smoky grey-mauve, often showing several of these colors at once in the same cluster. Exact introduction date and breeder are not reliably documented, as with many roses from this era. It flowers once in early summer, carries a strong fragrance, and forms a compact, dense shrub typical of the Gallica class, needing little more than removal of dead wood after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the heavy blooms benefit from some support to keep stems upright.

directions: Marie Louise is a Damask rose historically recorded as growing in the gardens of Malmaison in 1813, during the era of Empress Josephine. Its large, very double, clear pink blooms are so densely packed with petals that they often nod under their own weight, releasing the rich, classic damask fragrance long prized for perfumery. It flowers once, in a single heavy flush in early summer, on a lax, arching shrub that benefits from light staking. Routine removal of dead or crossing wood after bloom is all the pruning it requires.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most old Damasks this one reliably produces a second bloom in autumn.

directions: Also called the Autumn Damask, Quatre Saisons is one of the oldest rose cultivars still in general cultivation, documented in European gardens since medieval times with origins reaching further back toward the ancient Mediterranean world. Its semi-double to double, clear pink blooms carry an intense damask fragrance, and it is notable among old Damasks for genuinely repeating bloom in late summer and autumn rather than flowering only once. This trait made it historically important as a parent in the development of modern reblooming roses. It is tough, cold-hardy, and needs only routine removal of dead wood after each bloom flush.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this striped centifolia is also sold under the names Cottage Maid and Centifolia Variegata.

directions: Village Maid is a striped Centifolia of Dutch origin, documented in commerce by the 1840s and also sold under the names Cottage Maid and Centifolia Variegata. Its large, loosely double blooms are striped lilac-pink and blush white over the classic cupped, many-petaled Centifolia form, carrying the heavy old-rose fragrance the class is named for. It flowers once, in early summer, on a lax, arching shrub that benefits from some support. Routine removal of dead or crossing wood after bloom is its only real pruning need.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact centifolia needs less support than many lax-caned types in its class.

directions: Raised by Vibert in France in 1835, Blanchefleur is a Centifolia bearing very double, densely quartered blooms that open blush pink and fade to near white, packed with the strong old-rose fragrance typical of the class. It is more compact and self-supporting than many lax Centifolias, forming a tidy, well-branched shrub. It flowers once, in a single heavy early-summer flush, and tolerates average garden soil without special care. Only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after bloom is needed.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; among moss roses this cultivar is valued for its unusually large flowers.

directions: Introduced in France in 1852, Gloire des Mousseux is among the largest-flowered of the moss roses, bearing clear pink, very double, quartered blooms heavily clothed in soft, resinous, balsam-scented moss on the buds and sepals, the hallmark trait of the moss rose group. It flowers once, in a single abundant flush in early summer, and remains one of the moss roses most widely offered by heritage rose nurseries today. The vigorous, upright shrub tolerates average soil and needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; grown chiefly for its unusually dark, velvety flower color among moss roses.

directions: Introduced in France in 1854, Capitaine John Ingram is a moss rose bearing dark maroon-purple double blooms that age toward violet, with dense, dark moss covering the buds and sepals. It flowers once, in a compact early-summer flush, and carries a strong fragrance typical of the moss class. Its unusually deep, velvety coloring sets it apart from the more common clear-pink moss roses of its era. It needs only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after bloom and tolerates average garden soil.

common_name: Empereur du Maroc Hybrid Perpetual Rose

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; bloom color is darkest in cool weather and can bronze in summer heat.

directions: Introduced in France in 1858, Empereur du Maroc was famed in the Victorian era as one of the darkest roses then available, its velvety blooms a deep maroon that shades almost to black in cool weather, with moderate fragrance. As a Hybrid Perpetual it repeats bloom through the growing season, though its flowering can be sparser and less reliable than its contemporaries, a trait often noted by period rose growers. The upright, compact shrub needs average garden soil and benefits from deadheading to encourage repeat flushes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; striping can be more pronounced in cooler spring and fall flushes.

directions: Vick's Caprice appeared as a sport of the Hybrid Perpetual 'Archiduchesse Elisabeth d'Autriche' and was introduced in the United States by James Vick in the late 1880s. Its large, fragrant blooms are soft pink irregularly striped and flecked with lavender and white, with no two flowers marked exactly alike. As a Hybrid Perpetual it repeats bloom through the season, and it remains one of the few 19th-century striped roses still regularly offered by heritage rose nurseries. The upright shrub appreciates deadheading between flushes and average, well-drained garden soil.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; well suited to low hedging or edging because of its compact, nearly thornless habit.

directions: Raised by Alegatiere in France in 1888, Marie Pavie is a Polyantha bearing dense clusters of small, very fragrant, blush-white double blooms that open from pink-tinged buds. Unlike most once-blooming old roses, Polyanthas repeat bloom continuously through the growing season, and Marie Pavie is especially free-flowering. Its compact, nearly thornless habit has made it a popular low hedge and edging rose in gardens today, much as it was over a century ago. It needs only light shaping and routine removal of spent blooms to keep flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; forms a mounded, nearly thornless dwarf shrub well suited to borders.

directions: Little White Pet was discovered by Peter Henderson in the United States in 1879 as a dwarf, repeat-flowering sport of the once-blooming climber 'Felicite Perpetue'. It bears abundant clusters of small, pompon-form white double blooms opening from pink-tinged buds, carried on a compact, nearly thornless, mounded shrub rather than a climbing cane. Unlike its once-blooming climbing parent, it flowers continuously through the season, and it is often grown and sold as a Polyantha because of this dwarf, repeat-blooming habit. It needs only light shaping and tolerates average garden soil.
